rows: Fast chronological reconstruction view. MR62 = 1962 Missal/Ritus; RG60 = 1960 General Rubrics governing the 1962 regime. Exact source-level claims remain in Evidence Ledger.

For Solemn Mass, O'Connell's suggested congregational ceremonial has all stand during the entrance procession until the sacred ministers salute the altar; at Low Community Mass the people stand as the celebrant enters.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
At the Asperges all stand, join in the chant, and sign themselves when sprinkled.
Walsh: stand at High Mass Asperges.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
Sign of the Cross / Judica me

MR62 — The 1962 Ritus begins Low Mass at the foot of the altar with the sign of the Cross and preparatory prayers; exact omissions depend on the Mass/day.
RG60 — Rubrics 424–425: Judica, its antiphon, the Confiteor/absolution and related foot-of-altar prayers are the normal opening, with explicit omissions for processional-integrated Masses; Judica alone is omitted in Passiontide seasonal Masses and Requiem.

At Low Community Mass the people may kneel and say the opening prayers with the priest, or remain standing for a suitable entrance hymn/psalm or silent prayer; these options end before Introit/Kyrie as applicable.
Walsh: Low Mass kneel; High Mass kneel at beginning.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 424 includes the Confiteor and absolution in the normal opening at sung and Low Mass, but omits the whole opening cluster in specified Masses following preceding rites/processions.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 424 governs the opening Confiteor/absolution complex and its specified omissions.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
Ascent to altar / Aufer a nobis / Oramus te
RG60 — Rubric 424 explicitly names Aufer a nobis and Oramus te among the prayers omitted together with the foot-of-altar preparation in specified processional-integrated Masses.
Walsh: remain kneeling in High until Gloria; Low normally kneels.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 426: incensations required at Solemn Mass may also be performed at Missa Cantata.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 427 prescribes the Entrance antiphon with psalm verse and Gloria Patri, followed by repetition of the antiphon, subject to stated exceptions.
At Solemn Mass the Introit is sung as the ministers enter; after the ministers salute the altar the people kneel unless they themselves are singing the Introit.
Walsh: kneeling in opening High-Mass phase; Low kneeling.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 430 specifies the ninefold Kyrie: Kyrie three times, Christe three times, Kyrie three times.
At Solemn Mass the people stand while singing Kyrie; if the ministers sit during the chant, the people may sit also. At Low Community Mass they stand and answer Kyrie.
Walsh: same opening posture; sit if celebrant sits in prolonged sung Kyrie.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubrics 431–432 specify when Gloria is said or omitted; among the omissions are Masses with violet vestments and Masses of the Dead.
At Solemn Mass the people stand for the sung Gloria but may sit when the ministers sit; at Low Community Mass they stand and recite Gloria with the priest after his intonation.
Walsh: stand at intonation; sit when celebrant sits.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
The congregation normally stands for the Collect and responses; at most Masses in violet vestments and at Requiem Mass they kneel for Collects and Postcommunions.
Walsh: High stand for sung prayers; Low kneel.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 466 places the Epistle after the prayers with Deo gratias; in sung Masses rubric 473 removes from the celebrant what a subdeacon or lector proclaims by office.
At Solemn Mass the faithful sit for Lessons/Epistle; at Low Community Mass they are seated while reading/listening to the Epistle.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 469: the Gradual follows the Epistle, then Alleluia with its verse or the Tract according to the Missal.
At Solemn Mass the faithful sit for the Gradual; if they themselves sing the chant they stand. At Low Community Mass they may read it seated or use a suitable short psalm/hymn.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 469 orders Gradual then Alleluia or Tract; this is part of the scriptural/chant sequence before the Gospel.
O'Connell groups Alleluia/Tract with the interlection chants: faithful sit while listening, but stand if they themselves sing them.
Walsh: High sit until Gospel transition.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 470 places the Sequence before the last Alleluia or after the Tract and gives its votive-Mass omission rule.
O'Connell groups the Sequence with the interlection chants: faithful sit while listening, but stand if they themselves sing it.
Walsh: High sit during chant phase.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
Walsh: Solemn — no stand for celebrant's private Gospel.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — At the Gospel the celebrant signs the book and then forehead, lips and breast before proclaiming it; sung-Mass ministerial topology is governed separately.
RG60 — Rubric 471 gives the Gospel dialogue/formula; rubric 473 states that in sung Masses anything proclaimed by deacon, subdeacon or lector by virtue of office is omitted by the celebrant.
At Solemn Mass all stand when the Gospel procession moves; they answer and make the small signs of the Cross. At Low Community Mass the people stand and respond before and after the Gospel.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
MR62 — The three small crosses are prescribed for the liturgical minister proclaiming the Gospel; this source does not create a universal lay rubric to imitate them.
O'Connell explicitly directs the congregation at Solemn Mass to make the small sign of the Cross on forehead, lips, and breast at the Gospel.
Guéranger lay Ordinary documents three small crosses as traditional custom; not a universal 1962 lay rubric.
Ministerial Gospel crosses are rubrical; lay imitation is traditional custom, not established as universal 1962 lay law.

MR62 — The celebrant recites the Credo when prescribed; in sung Mass the choir's singing and celebrant's recitation can be distinct in time.
RG60 — Rubrics 475–476 determine when the Creed is said or omitted. Rubric 518 separately governs the celebrant's genuflection at Et incarnatus in sung Mass.
At Solemn Mass the congregation sings the Creed standing, but may sit when the ministers sit; at Low Community Mass they stand and may recite the Creed with the celebrant.
Walsh: stand for priest's recited Credo; sit when celebrant sits while choir continues.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
Et incarnatus est / Et homo factus est

MR62 — The celebrant genuflects at Et incarnatus est when reciting the Creed. When the choir sings the words, his action depends on whether he is standing or seated; at the three Christmas Masses and Annunciation all kneel during the sung words.
RG60 — Rubric 518: celebrant always genuflects when he recites Et incarnatus; when it is sung he genuflects again if standing, or makes a profound uncovered bow if seated; at the three Christmas Masses and Annunciation everyone kneels while the words are sung.

At the celebrant's recited Et incarnatus all genuflect. When the words are sung, those standing genuflect while those seated bow; on Christmas and the Annunciation everyone kneels. Low Community Mass has the people genuflect with the priest.
Walsh: kneel/bend knee at Incarnatus in traditional scheme; local variation noted. 1962 rule is actor/state/feast dependent.
Actor/state/feast dependent. Do not collapse celebrant, choir and faithful practice into one posture.
RG60 — Rubric 477: after Creed, or after Gospel/homily if there is no Creed, Dominus vobiscum, Oremus and the Offertory antiphon follow.

At Solemn Mass the congregation sits after Oremus for the Offertory; at Low Community Mass they likewise may sit after the greeting/Oremus and may recite the Offertory antiphon or use suitable offering prayers/hymns.
Walsh: High sit during Offertory; Low generally kneel.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 479 sends the offering of Host and Chalice and what follows to the Ordinary of the Mass.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 479 governs the offering/preparation of Host and Chalice according to the Ordinary.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 479 governs the offering of the Chalice according to the Ordinary.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

At Solemn Mass the congregation stands when the deacon comes to incense the clergy/people, bows before and after being incensed, then sits. Separately, O'Connell states that incense is now permitted at Sung Mass and used as at Solemn Mass except for the post-Gospel incensation of the celebrant.
Walsh: stand when congregation is incensed at Solemn Mass.
Walsh-era Missa Cantata normally lacked incense; 1962 permits incense at sung Mass without sacred ministers.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
At Low Community Mass the people stand for Orate fratres and may give the Latin response; O'Connell notes that standing when directly addressed is more correct.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubrics 480–481: the Secret is said secretly; the conclusion of the last Secret remains secret until Per omnia saecula saeculorum, which is said in a clear voice.
The Secret remains a priestly secret prayer; Low Community Mass faithful follow it in their missals and answer Amen when the conclusion is spoken aloud.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — The Preface is said/sung audibly after the dialogue; it leads directly into the Sanctus and Canon.
RG60 — Rubrics 482–499 govern the Preface; rubric 511 classifies Preface among the clear-voice parts of Low Mass, and rubric 513 specifies its sung treatment at Solemn Mass.
O'Connell classifies the Preface among the clear/audible parts of Low Mass; congregational guidance has the people rise/listen and make the dialogue responses.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — Sanctus immediately precedes the Canon; the server's bell belongs to the 1962 altar-bell choreography.
RG60 — Rubric 500 places the silent Canon immediately after Preface and Sanctus; rubric 511 makes Sanctus-Benedictus a clear-voice part at Low Mass.
Sanctus-Benedictus is among the audible parts; at Solemn/Community Mass the people sing/recite it and then kneel for the Canon.
Walsh: kneel from Sanctus through Communion.
Historical manuals differ on bell legal status/details; 1962 official text controls.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — The Canon is recited in the prescribed low voice beginning with Te igitur.
RG60 — Rubric 500: after Preface and Sanctus the Canon of the Mass is said silently. Rubrics 511–512 define clear versus secret voice.

O'Connell states that the Canon begins with Te igitur in the secret voice; the Canon remains secret except Nobis quoque and the concluding Per omnia. Low Community Mass faithful pray silently through it, kneeling through the Consecration and normally standing afterward; penitential/Requiem Masses retain kneeling.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
MR62 — Shortly before the Consecration the minister gives a warning with the small bell.
In the server ceremonial O'Connell places a warning bell at Hanc igitur shortly before the Consecration.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
Britt: Hanc igitur bell permissible in older law; 1962 Ritus explicitly prescribes a warning shortly before Consecration.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
MR62 — After the consecratory words over the Host the priest immediately adores by genuflecting.
O'Connell's Consecration choreography is atomic: consecratory words are pronounced distinctly and reverently; the Host is then adored by genuflection before being elevated.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
MR62 — First genuflection follows the Host's consecration before the elevation.
The first genuflection follows the Host Consecration before the elevation.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
MR62 — The priest rises and elevates the Sacred Host, showing it to the people for adoration; the bell is rung three times, or continuously until the Host is lowered.

The Sacred Host is elevated so it can be clearly seen and adored by the people; O'Connell says the Church desires the faithful to look at the Host. Congregational guidance explicitly says to bow but look up at the elevations.
Walsh: kneel/adore; Augustine says precise devotional acts vary by country/custom.
Britt's common signal mapping is historical ceremonial implementation; 1962 text permits three rings or continuous ringing at elevation.
MR62 — After replacing the Host on the corporal the priest genuflects again.
After lowering/replacing the Host the celebrant genuflects again.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
MR62 — The Chalice is consecrated with the prescribed words, followed by the adoration/elevation sequence.
O'Connell gives the Chalice consecration as a distinct atomic action followed by genuflection, elevation for adoration, replacement, pall and second genuflection.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
MR62 — The priest genuflects after the Chalice consecration before its elevation.
After the Chalice consecration the celebrant replaces the Chalice and genuflects before elevating it.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
MR62 — The priest elevates the Chalice and shows it; the bell is rung three times, or continuously until it is lowered.
The Chalice is slowly raised high enough to be clearly seen; O'Connell says it is held aloft for the adoration of the people. Congregational guidance says the faithful look up at it.
Walsh: kneel/adore; Augustine says precise devotional acts vary by country/custom.
MR62 — After replacing the Chalice the priest genuflects again.
After the Chalice is lowered, covered with the pall, the celebrant genuflects again.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — Nobis quoque is one of the Canon moments said in a somewhat raised voice relative to the secret Canon; the celebrant strikes his breast.
RG60 — Rubric 511 explicitly includes Nobis quoque peccatoribus among the clear-voice parts of Low Mass, while the remainder of the Canon is secret except its public conclusion.
O'Connell says Nobis quoque peccatoribus is now said aloud; the celebrant stands erect, left hand on altar, and strikes his breast with the right, then continues silently.
Guéranger: faithful customarily strike breast with priest; Britt says server does not — actor-specific.
Guéranger says faithful strike breast; Britt explicitly says server does not. Gesture belongs to actor, not text globally.
RG60 — Rubric 511 includes the Canon's Per omnia saecula saeculorum among the clear-voice parts.
O'Connell lists Per omnia saecula saeculorum at the Canon conclusion among the audible parts, marking the public conclusion of the secret Canon.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — The Canon concludes and the Pater Noster begins audibly/sung according to Mass form.
RG60 — Rubric 511 places the Pater noster with its introduction among the clear-voice parts; rubric 513 specifies its singing at Solemn Mass.
Pater noster is audible; O'Connell's congregational guidance has the people stand and, in the permitted Community Mass form, recite it in Latin with the celebrant.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 511 includes Agnus Dei among the clear-voice parts of Low Mass.
At Solemn/Community Mass the people sing or recite Agnus Dei and then kneel to prepare for Communion.
Walsh: kneeling phase; lay breast-strike should be separately sourced rather than inferred.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
Pax is ministerial in these sources; no basis here for modern congregational exchange-of-peace choreography.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
RG60 — Rubric 511 newly includes the priest's Domine non sum dignus before his Communion among the clear-voice parts.

O'Connell says the priest's Domine non sum dignus is his private prayer before his own Communion; the server does not thereby acquire a lay/minister gesture. O'Connell also says the former bell usage at the priest's Dnsd should cease when Communion of the faithful is expected.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
Britt says server does not strike at priest's Dnsd; older bell custom exists; do not copy priest's gesture to everyone.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
Warning bell before Communion of faithful
MR62 — If the faithful are to communicate, the minister gives a warning with the bell shortly beforehand.
When faithful are to receive Communion, O'Connell directs one warning ring shortly before Communion, recommending shortly after Agnus Dei so communicants approach before the celebrant's Communion.
Walsh posture remains kneeling; 1962 has conditional Communion warning bell.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
Second Confiteor before Communion — historical / 1962 status

MR62 — The additional Confiteor/Misereatur/Indulgentiam immediately before Communion of the faithful is not part of the normative 1962 sequence; the 1960 General Rubrics suppressed it.
RG60 — Rubric 503: when Communion is distributed during Mass, after the celebrant receives the Precious Blood the Confiteor and absolution are omitted; the rite goes directly to Ecce Agnus Dei and Domine non sum dignus.

O'Connell explicitly states that the Confiteor which formerly signaled communicants 'is no longer said.' He likewise says the bell should no longer be rung at the priest's Domine non sum dignus because that was never a rubric, merely usage.
1962: no second Confiteor as normative rite; older B/A31/O'Brien explicitly include it.
Major reform boundary: B/A31/O'Brien include second Confiteor; 1962 suppresses it.

MR62 — After the priest's Communion, when the faithful communicate, the rite proceeds to Ecce Agnus Dei and the Communion formulas without the old second Confiteor.
RG60 — Rubric 503 orders Ecce Agnus Dei three times after the priest's Precious Blood, with the Confiteor/absolution omitted.
After the celebrant consumes the Precious Blood he prepares the ciborium/paten and, after the required genuflection, turns to say Ecce Agnus Dei; no second Confiteor intervenes.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — Domine non sum dignus is said three times in preparation for Communion of the faithful.
RG60 — Rubric 503 orders Domine non sum dignus three times before distribution of Communion.
O'Connell says Ecce Agnus Dei is followed by Domine non sum dignus three times; the entire prayer is aloud and communicants may say it aloud with the priest.
Traditional communicant humility/breast-strike strongly documented; classify by source/actor.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — Communion of the faithful follows the priest's Communion and precedes the ablutions.
RG60 — Rubrics 502–503: the proper time for Communion of the faithful is during Mass after the celebrant's Communion; after the Precious Blood and omission of Confiteor/absolution, Communion is distributed immediately after Ecce Agnus Dei / triple Domine non sum dignus.
O'Connell treats Communion of the faithful as following the priest's Communion sequence; Community Mass guidance has communicants approach promptly at the warning bell and recite the triple Dnsd.
Walsh: kneeling through Communion in traditional sung-Mass posture.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.
MR62 — After Communion and any distribution to the faithful, the priest performs the prescribed ablutions/purifications.
After Communion, O'Connell says those who have not communicated may sit during the ablutions until the Postcommunion greeting.
Walsh: sit after Communion while priest purifies/covers chalice.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — In sung Mass the Communion antiphon is sung by the choir; it can overlap the ministerial Communion sequence depending on form.
RG60 — Rubric 504 governs the Communion antiphon after the Canon and the intervening Communion rite.

O'Connell says that when communicants are present the Communion antiphon is sung during distribution and may be prolonged with psalm verses; if none communicate it is sung while the celebrant receives.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — Postcommunion prayer(s) follow the Communion antiphon/ablutions and are said or sung according to form.
RG60 — Rubric 505 says Postcommunions follow the same number, manner and order as the prayers at the beginning of Mass; rubric 506 adds the Prayer over the People on specified Lenten/Passion ferias.
Faithful stand for Dominus vobiscum/Postcommunion and respond; at violet/Requiem Masses they kneel.
Walsh: stand for final prayers; Requiem differs.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — The concluding formula depends on the Mass: Ite missa est, Benedicamus Domino, or Requiescant in pace as rubrically applicable.
RG60 — Rubric 507: normally Ite missa est / Deo gratias; Benedicamus Domino where Mass is followed by a procession; Requiescant in pace / Amen in Masses of the Dead; Easter-octave seasonal Masses add double Alleluia.
The congregation answers the dismissal: Deo gratias to Ite missa est, Amen to Requiescant in pace.
Walsh: stand in final prayer/dismissal phase.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — The blessing is not given in every case; the Ritus states the relevant exceptions in the final rites.
RG60 — Rubric 508: the blessing follows Placeat and is omitted only when Benedicamus Domino or Requiescant in pace has been used.
O'Connell directs the people to kneel for the blessing, sign themselves, answer Amen, then stand. If Benedicamus Domino is used there is no blessing and they remain standing.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

MR62 — The normal Last Gospel is John 1:1–14, with restricted 1962 omissions/exceptions; the celebrant genuflects at Et Verbum caro factum est.
RG60 — Rubrics 509–510: the normal Last Gospel is John 1; Palm Sunday retains a special proper Last Gospel when Mass does not follow the palms, and the Last Gospel is completely omitted in a restricted set of cases.
O'Connell directs all to stand for the Last Gospel and genuflect with the priest at Et Verbum caro factum est; Low Community Mass likewise remains standing as the priest leaves.
Walsh: stand for Last Gospel; genuflect at Et Verbum caro factum est.
Older sources reflect broad proper-Last-Gospel system; 1962 sharply restricts it.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
No major conflict yet logged; source-date, rite-scope and actor-scope still apply.

Compact side-by-side practical-source comparison. MR62 = 1962 Missal/Ritus. The General Rubrics (RG60) are kept in the dedicated Primary Rubrics sheet and Evidence Ledger to avoid widening this matrix.

For Solemn Mass, O'Connell's suggested congregational ceremonial has all stand during the entrance procession until the sacred ministers salute the altar; at Low Community Mass the people stand as the celebrant enters.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.
At the Asperges all stand, join in the chant, and sign themselves when sprinkled.
At High Mass, faithful stand for the Asperges.
Walsh: stand at High Mass Asperges.
Sign of the Cross / Judica me
The 1962 Ritus begins Low Mass at the foot of the altar with the sign of the Cross and preparatory prayers; exact omissions depend on the Mass/day.

At Low Community Mass the people may kneel and say the opening prayers with the priest, or remain standing for a suitable entrance hymn/psalm or silent prayer; these options end before Introit/Kyrie as applicable.
Server makes the full Sign of the Cross deliberately; Britt gives exact hand placement and forehead–breast–left shoulder–right shoulder execution.
Low Mass: faithful ordinarily kneel throughout except at the Gospels. High Mass: kneel from the beginning until the Gloria.
Augustine treats bodily actions/posture as integral to liturgical action and discusses the Sign of the Cross as a sacramental gesture; he distinguishes standing, kneeling and sitting traditions.
Walsh: Low Mass kneel; High Mass kneel at beginning.
During the priest's Confiteor the server remains kneeling erect and does not strike his breast.
Low Mass: faithful ordinarily kneel throughout except at the Gospels. High Mass: kneel from the beginning until the Gloria.

Low Mass: faithful ordinarily kneel throughout except at the Gospels. High Mass: kneel from the beginning until the Gloria.

Low Mass: faithful ordinarily kneel throughout except at the Gospels. High Mass: kneel from the beginning until the Gloria.

At High Mass, stand when the Gloria is intoned; sit when the celebrant sits.
Walsh: stand at intonation; sit when celebrant sits.
The congregation normally stands for the Collect and responses; at most Masses in violet vestments and at Requiem Mass they kneel for Collects and Postcommunions.
At High Mass, stand for sung prayers; Walsh notes Requiem exceptions. At Low Mass the general posture remains kneeling.

At Solemn High Mass, do not stand merely because the celebrant privately reads the Gospel.

At the Gospel the celebrant signs the book and then forehead, lips and breast before proclaiming it; sung-Mass ministerial topology is governed separately.
At Solemn Mass all stand when the Gospel procession moves; they answer and make the small signs of the Cross. At Low Community Mass the people stand and respond before and after the Gospel.
At Solemn Mass the acolytes follow the thurifer to the public Gospel; while carrying candles they do not make the normal signs/genuflections/bows during the Gospel.
Stand for the Gospel; at Solemn High Mass the posture cue is the Gospel sung by the deacon, not the celebrant's private reading.
Wynne's Ordinary moves from the Gospel to the Creed, presenting the Gospel as the public proclamation encountered by the faithful.
Augustine's general posture discussion notes sitting for Scripture except the Gospel/homily in the historical discipline he describes.
The three small crosses are prescribed for the liturgical minister proclaiming the Gospel; this source does not create a universal lay rubric to imitate them.
O'Connell explicitly directs the congregation at Solemn Mass to make the small sign of the Cross on forehead, lips, and breast at the Gospel.
At each Gospel the ordinary server makes three small crosses on forehead, lips and breast with the thumb; Britt gives exact execution details.
Stand for the Gospel; at Solemn High Mass the posture cue is the Gospel sung by the deacon, not the celebrant's private reading.
Guéranger lay Ordinary documents three small crosses as traditional custom; not a universal 1962 lay rubric.
The celebrant recites the Credo when prescribed; in sung Mass the choir's singing and celebrant's recitation can be distinct in time.
At Solemn Mass the congregation sings the Creed standing, but may sit when the ministers sit; at Low Community Mass they stand and may recite the Creed with the celebrant.
Missa Cantata/Solemn server posture differs between celebrant's recitation and choir's sung Credo; acolytes can sit or stand at the bench depending configuration.
Stand while the priest recites the Credo; sit when he goes to the bench while the choir continues.
Wynne places the Nicene Creed immediately after the Gospel and gives its historical doctrinal background.
Augustine notes approved liturgists' rules and the role of interpretation/custom in postures; his Missa Cantata discussion says the celebrant may sit during Kyrie, Gloria and Credo.
Walsh: stand for priest's recited Credo; sit when celebrant sits while choir continues.
Et incarnatus est / Et homo factus est

The celebrant genuflects at Et incarnatus est when reciting the Creed. When the choir sings the words, his action depends on whether he is standing or seated; at the three Christmas Masses and Annunciation all kneel during the sung words.

At the celebrant's recited Et incarnatus all genuflect. When the words are sung, those standing genuflect while those seated bow; on Christmas and the Annunciation everyone kneels. Low Community Mass has the people genuflect with the priest.

Britt records a kneeling norm for servers during Credo in Low/Missa Cantata, but cites O'Connell noting an approved standing alternative; at sung Et incarnatus action depends on whether servers are standing/seated and on custom.
Kneel at Et incarnatus / Et homo factus est in Walsh's traditional scheme; at Low Mass he notes that some places stand for the Credo and bend the knee at Et homo factus est.
Walsh: kneel/bend knee at Incarnatus in traditional scheme; local variation noted. 1962 rule is actor/state/feast dependent.

At Solemn Mass the congregation sits after Oremus for the Offertory; at Low Community Mass they likewise may sit after the greeting/Oremus and may recite the Offertory antiphon or use suitable offering prayers/hymns.
At High Mass, sit during the Offertory until the Preface. Low Mass remains under the general kneeling custom.
Wynne marks the transition from Creed to Offertory as a distinct new part of Mass.
Walsh: High sit during Offertory; Low generally kneel.
At Offertory, server/acolyte actions begin when the chalice veil is removed; wine and water are brought in ordered choreography.
At High Mass, sit during the Offertory until the Preface. Low Mass remains under the general kneeling custom.
Wynne describes the offering of the bread/Host as a distinct Offertory action.
No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.

At High Mass, sit during the Offertory until the Preface. Low Mass remains under the general kneeling custom.

No separate lay-posture claim yet located; do not infer from priest/server choreography.

Solemn Offertory incensation proceeds altar → celebrant/clergy/subdeacon → deacon → MC/acolytes → people; thurifer then departs with torchbearers.

At Solemn High Mass, stand when the congregation itself is being incensed.
• Walsh's older account treats Missa Cantata as a sung Mass without deacon/subdeacon and, in his period, without incense — a historical contrast to 1962 permission.
Augustine says authorities were not unanimous on Missa Cantata ceremonial and describes a topology with celebrant, servers, thurifer and choir.

Servers/acolytes bring basin, water and towel for the Lavabo and make prescribed bows in the manual's choreography.

O'Connell classifies the Preface among the clear/audible parts of Low Mass; congregational guidance has the people rise/listen and make the dialogue responses.

Augustine says Preface is said in the loud voice corresponding to what would be sung at High Mass.
Sanctus immediately precedes the Canon; the server's bell belongs to the 1962 altar-bell choreography.
Sanctus-Benedictus is among the audible parts; at Solemn/Community Mass the people sing/recite it and then kneel for the Canon.

Walsh: kneel from Sanctus through Communion.

Low Community Mass faithful pray silently through it, kneeling through the Consecration and normally standing afterward; penitential/Requiem Masses retain kneeling.
At High Mass, Walsh's traditional lay track kneels from the Sanctus through Communion.

At High Mass, Walsh's traditional lay track kneels from the Sanctus through Communion.

Second Confiteor before Communion — historical / 1962 status
The additional Confiteor/Misereatur/Indulgentiam immediately before Communion of the faithful is not part of the normative 1962 sequence; the 1960 General Rubrics suppressed it.

O'Connell explicitly states that the Confiteor which formerly signaled communicants 'is no longer said.' He likewise says the bell should no longer be rung at the priest's Domine non sum dignus because that was never a rubric, merely usage.
If Communion is distributed, Britt has servers arrange the Communion cloth, return, kneel and recite a second Confiteor before Communion.
At High Mass, Walsh's traditional lay track kneels from the Sanctus through Communion.

1962: no second Confiteor as normative rite; older B/A31/O'Brien explicitly include it.
After the priest's Communion, when the faithful communicate, the rite proceeds to Ecce Agnus Dei and the Communion formulas without the old second Confiteor.
After the celebrant consumes the Precious Blood he prepares the ciborium/paten and, after the required genuflection, turns to say Ecce Agnus Dei; no second Confiteor intervenes.
At High Mass, Walsh's traditional lay track kneels from the Sanctus through Communion.
In Augustine's older sequence Ecce Agnus Dei follows the Confiteor/Misereatur/Indulgentiam complex.

Wynne separately describes distribution of Holy Communion to the faithful after the priest's Communion.

After Communion, O'Connell says those who have not communicated may sit during the ablutions until the Postcommunion greeting.
Britt gives two-server ablution choreography: wine/water are brought, Missal is transferred back, and servers return to position.
After Communion, sit while the priest purifies and covers the chalice.
Wynne describes ablutions as first rinsing the chalice with wine, then wine and water over the priest's fingers.
Walsh: sit after Communion while priest purifies/covers chalice.
In sung Mass the Communion antiphon is sung by the choir; it can overlap the ministerial Communion sequence depending on form.

O'Connell says that when communicants are present the Communion antiphon is sung during distribution and may be prolonged with psalm verses; if none communicate it is sung while the celebrant receives.
After Communion, sit while the priest purifies and covers the chalice.
Postcommunion prayer(s) follow the Communion antiphon/ablutions and are said or sung according to form.
Faithful stand for Dominus vobiscum/Postcommunion and respond; at violet/Requiem Masses they kneel.
Stand for the final prayers / concluding phase before the blessing.

The concluding formula depends on the Mass: Ite missa est, Benedicamus Domino, or Requiescant in pace as rubrically applicable.
The congregation answers the dismissal: Deo gratias to Ite missa est, Amen to Requiescant in pace.
Stand for the final prayers / concluding phase before the blessing.
Walsh: stand in final prayer/dismissal phase.
The blessing is not given in every case; the Ritus states the relevant exceptions in the final rites.
O'Connell directs the people to kneel for the blessing, sign themselves, answer Amen, then stand. If Benedicamus Domino is used there is no blessing and they remain standing.
Wynne places the final blessing before the Last Gospel in the concluding sequence.
The normal Last Gospel is John 1:1–14, with restricted 1962 omissions/exceptions; the celebrant genuflects at Et Verbum caro factum est.
O'Connell directs all to stand for the Last Gospel and genuflect with the priest at Et Verbum caro factum est; Low Community Mass likewise remains standing as the priest leaves.
Older Britt material includes the broader pre-1962 proper-Last-Gospel system and server choreography; this must not control 1962 exceptions.
Stand for the Last Gospel and genuflect at Et Verbum caro factum est.

tabs.name: Interpretation Matrix
rows: This sheet answers 'what does each interpretive author say at this Mass moment?' It is not a rubrical ranking. St Vincent is Dominican-Rite and St Francis is an attributed private devotional method.
Lasance frames assistance at Mass by uniting oneself with the priest's offering and the four ends: adoration, satisfaction/reparation, thanksgiving and petition.

St. Leonard explicitly permits different holy methods of hearing Mass; his 'third method' divides the Mass into four periods corresponding to four debts owed to God rather than requiring a word-for-word private prayer track.
The priest's emergence from the sacristy is interpreted as Christ's Nativity/public manifestation; the underlying work presents the Mass as an epitome of Christ's whole life, not only His Passion.
Sign of the Cross / Judica me
Lasance supplies acts of adoration/contrition around opening prayers and Confiteor, but does not make them a mandatory synchronized private-prayer script.

Knox interprets Judica and the opening preparation as the Church separating herself from the profane world before approaching the altar; he immediately distinguishes this from the more personal Confiteor.
Foot of altar → Christ enters Gethsemane / prayer in the garden.
Lasance supplies acts of adoration/contrition around opening prayers and Confiteor, but does not make them a mandatory synchronized private-prayer script.
Knox reads the Confiteor as awareness of one's sinfulness and unworthiness to approach God, rather than a detailed examination of particular sins.
At the beginning, especially around the Confiteor, St. Leonard recommends contrition, asking pardon, and invoking the Holy Spirit and Our Lady before entering the four-part method.
The priest's Confiteor symbolizes Christ's Circumcision/humility in appearing under the likeness of a sinner.
Confiteor → Christ prostrate in the garden and the bloody sweat.
Lasance supplies acts of adoration/contrition around opening prayers and Confiteor, but does not make them a mandatory synchronized private-prayer script.
Ascent to altar / Aufer a nobis / Oramus te
The priest's approach/kiss of the altar after Confiteor is linked to the coming of the Magi and their offerings.
Priest kisses altar → Judas' betrayal by a kiss; movement to Epistle side → Christ dragged to prison.
O'Brien treats the Introit as giving the scope/key or dominant sentiment of the Mass of the day and traces its ceremonial history.
Guéranger explains that the Introit originally belonged to the choir during the entrance; later priestly recitation reflects the development of Low Mass and subsequent duplication at sung Mass.
Lasance provides an Introit-associated devotional prayer/psalm, while explicitly saying the faithful need not say every supplied prayer.
Knox interprets the Introit as the point where the priest moves from preparatory hesitation into the liturgy of the day.
The Introit at the Epistle side symbolizes the Presentation in the Temple; the surrounding ministers receive further symbolic identifications.
Introit → Christ receives a blow at the house of Annas.
O'Brien gives a historical study of the Kyrie, including its Greek form and Eastern/Western background.

tabs.name: Primary Rubrics
rows: PRIMARY RUBRICS — GENERAL RUBRICS OF THE ROMAN MISSAL (1960)

Controlling rubrical layer translated contemporaneously by Patrick L. Murphy. This sheet isolates the general legal rules from the 1962 Missal/Ritus ceremonial text. Posture §§520–524 applies to those in choir / celebrant roles and must not be silently converted into a universal lay-pew posture track.
Mass is public worship rendered to God in the name of Christ and the Church; avoid the expression 'Private Masses'.
Primary law — official 1960 Code in contemporary English translation
Sung vs Low; Solemn vs Cantata
Masses are sung or Low; sung with sacred ministers is Solemn/High Mass, sung without sacred ministers is Missa Cantata.
Mass by its nature requires all present to participate in the manner proper to each; detailed faithful participation is referred to the 1958 Instruction.
Normal foot-of-altar preparation is specified; the whole cluster or Judica alone is omitted in enumerated contexts.
Incensations required in Solemn Mass may also be performed in Missa Cantata.
Defines Entrance antiphon, ninefold Kyrie, and when Gloria is said or omitted.
Defines the chronological scriptural/chant sequence preceding and including the Gospel.
What deacon, subdeacon or lector sings/reads by office is omitted by celebrant.
Orders Offertory transition; Host/Chalice offering follows Ordinary; Secret is secret until clear-voice Per omnia.
After Preface and Sanctus the Canon is said silently as in the Order of Mass.
Proper time is after celebrant Communion; after Precious Blood Confiteor/absolution omitted; Ecce Agnus Dei and Domine non sum dignus three times, then distribution.
Defines Communion antiphon, Postcommunions, dismissal variants, blessing exceptions and restricted Last-Gospel exceptions.
Enumerates clear-voice parts and defines audible vs secret pronunciation.
Celebrant voice + omission of duplicated parts
Defines sung/clear/secret celebrant parts and requires omission of parts proclaimed by sacred ministers/lector.
Celebrant follows sung-Mass rules and performs sacred-minister sung parts; Epistle may be sung by lector, otherwise celebrant may read or sing.
Defines celebrant genuflections; at sung words he reacts when others sing; Et incarnatus has standing/seated/feast-dependent rules; ministers have role-specific exceptions.

These are choir/celebrant rules, not a universal congregational pew posture code. Includes Consecration, faithful Communion, penitential/Requiem kneeling, Incarnatus/Last Gospel genuflections, and sitting permissions.
